hook.line: You like the plan. You just have one small problem with it. *Pero* can sound like a flat no, so Bogotanos soften it.
hook.es: Me encantaría ir, solo que no tengo plata.
hook.en: I'd love to go, it's just that I have no money.

examples.es: El plan es bueno, solo que es un poco caro.
examples.en: The plan's good, it's just a bit expensive.

examples.es: Me encantaría ir, solo que no tengo plata.
examples.en: I'd love to go, it's just that I have no money.

examples.es: Tenía buena intención, solo que no me expliqué bien.
examples.en: I meant well, I just didn't explain myself properly.

examples.es: La casa es linda, solo que queda muy lejos.
examples.en: The house is lovely, it's just very far away.

examples.es: Quiero ayudarte, solo que hoy no puedo.
examples.en: I want to help you, it's just that I can't today.

examples.es: El café de Rosa es el mejor, solo que casi nadie lo conoce.
examples.en: Rosa's café is the best, it's just that hardly anyone knows it.

rule:
*Solo que* means "it's just that" or "only". It keeps what you said first true and adds one small limitation, often with a hint of apology.

*Pero* contradicts. *Solo que* qualifies. After a comma, *solo que* introduces a new full sentence: *me encantaría ir, solo que no tengo plata*.

Don't stack them: it is *solo que*, not *pero solo que*. And *solo* before a verb or noun is a different word: *solo quiero un tinto* means "I only want a coffee".
smallPrint: Teachers call *solo que* a conjunctive adverb, the softer cousin of *pero*.

readAndPick.es: Vale quiere venir, solo que está ocupada.
options: Vale wants to come, it's just that she's busy.
Vale wants to come because she's busy.
Vale only wants to come when she's busy.
I want a coffee, it's just that…
I only want a coffee.
I want a coffee for myself.

readAndPick.es: El hotel es lindo, solo que queda lejos.
options: The hotel is lovely, it's just far away.
The hotel is lovely, so it's far away.
The hotel is far away because it's lovely.

readAndPick.es: Quiero ir, solo que no puedo.
options: I want to go, so I can't.
I want to go, I just can't.
I can only go when I want.

readAndPick.es: Tomás solo llegó a las ocho.
options: Tomás arrived at eight, it's just that…
Tomás arrived at eight, so…
Tomás only arrived at eight.

readAndPick.es: La idea es buena, solo que necesita tiempo.
options: The idea is good, it's just that it needs time.
The idea is good because it needs time.
The idea is good, so it needs time.

readAndPick.es: Me gusta la casa, solo que es pequeña.
options: I like the house because it's small.
I like the house, it's just small.
I only like the house when it's small.

readAndPick.es: No es caro, solo que no tengo plata.
options: It's not expensive, it's just that I have no money.
It's not expensive, so I have no money.
It's expensive, only I have money.
Hernando only drinks black coffee.
Hernando drinks coffee, it's just that…
Hernando drinks coffee, so…

yourTurn.prompt: Pick the right words and type the whole sentence: *La casa es linda, ___ queda muy lejos.* (*solo que* or *porque*)
yourTurn.answer: La casa es linda, solo que queda muy lejos.
yourTurn.why: You are adding a small limitation to something good, which is what *solo que* does.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick the right words and type the whole sentence: *El plan es bueno, ___ es un poco caro.* (*solo que* or *por eso*)
yourTurn.answer: El plan es bueno, solo que es un poco caro.
yourTurn.why: *Por eso* gives a result; *solo que* adds a snag.

yourTurn.prompt: Type it in Spanish: I'd love to go, it's just that I have no money.
yourTurn.answer: Me encantaría ir, solo que no tengo plata.
accept: Me encantaría ir, solo que no tengo dinero.
yourTurn.why: *Solo que* sits after a comma and starts a new sentence.

yourTurn.prompt: Type it in Spanish: Rosa's café is the best, it's just that hardly anyone knows it.
yourTurn.answer: El café de Rosa es el mejor, solo que casi nadie lo conoce.
yourTurn.why: The first half stays true; *solo que* adds the limit.

yourTurn.prompt: Type it in Spanish: I want to help you, it's just that I can't today.
yourTurn.answer: Quiero ayudarte, solo que hoy no puedo.
accept: Quiero ayudarte, solo que no puedo hoy.

yourTurn.prompt: Join the two sentences with *solo que*: *Quiero ir. No tengo tiempo.*
yourTurn.answer: Quiero ir, solo que no tengo tiempo.
yourTurn.why: A comma and *solo que* replace the full stop.

yourTurn.prompt: Soften it with *solo que* instead of *pero*: *La idea es buena, pero necesita tiempo.*
yourTurn.answer: La idea es buena, solo que necesita tiempo.
yourTurn.why: *Solo que* swaps in for *pero* and sounds gentler.

pitfalls.wrong: El plan es bueno, pero solo que es caro.
pitfalls.right: El plan es bueno, solo que es caro.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Solo que* already does the job of *pero*, so you don't need both.

pitfalls.wrong: El plan es bueno solo que es caro.
pitfalls.right: El plan es bueno, solo que es caro.
pitfalls.why: Spanish puts a comma before *solo que*, like the pause in English.

pitfalls.right: Quiero ir, solo que no puedo.
pitfalls.why: English says "I just can't", but Spanish needs the *que* to join the second sentence.

personal: Tell us about something you like, with one small catch, using *solo que*.
